title: Jaggery in Nepali Is Sakhar. So What Is Sakhar in English?
seoTitle: Jaggery in Nepali: Sakhar (सख्खर), and What It Means
description: Jaggery in Nepali is sakhar (सख्खर). But sakhar in English is sugar if the word is Marathi. What jaggery is, and what it is called in Nepali and Hindi.
content:
A recipe says one cup of sakhar. Somebody in Kathmandu reaches for a dark block of jaggery. Somebody in Pune reaches for the white sugar tin. They are both reading the word correctly, and one of them is about to make something that tastes nothing like what the cook intended.

That is why sakhar in English, or jaggery in Nepali, is a harder question than it looks. The word means different things depending on which language is doing the talking. We make sakhar (सख्खर, also spelled sakhkhar) for a living in Sankhuwasabha, so we have a stake in the Nepali answer. We will give you the other answers straight.

> Jaggery in Nepali is sakhar (सख्खर), and sakhar in English is jaggery: unrefined cane sugar, boiled down and set as a hard brown block. But in Marathi, sakhar (साखर) means ordinary white sugar, and jaggery is gul (गूळ). In Hindi, jaggery is gur (गुड़). Check which language your recipe was written in before you buy anything.

## What Is Jaggery Called in Nepali?

Jaggery in Nepali is sakhar (सख्खर). In the Terai, and anywhere the block came up from the plains, you will also hear gur or gud (गुड़) for the same thing. White sugar is chini (चिनी), and nobody in a Nepali shop will confuse the two.

Two more words sit close by. Khudo (खुदो) is the liquid stage, before the juice is boiled hard enough to set. Chaku (चाकु) is a sweet made from sakhar, not sakhar itself.

## What Is Jaggery?

In Nepal, sakhar is jaggery. It is the juice of sugar cane, pressed, boiled in an iron kadhai until most of the water has gone, and poured into moulds to set. Nothing is spun out of it and nothing is bleached. The block that comes out is brown, hard and tastes of caramel.

Jaggery is the English word you will find on packets, in cookbooks and in most shops outside South Asia. The technical name is [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar), because what separates it from white sugar is that it never goes through a centrifuge. If you see NCS, panela or unrefined cane sugar on a label, it is the same family of product.

What sakhar is not, in Nepali, is white sugar. That is chini (चिनी). A Nepali kitchen keeps the two in different jars: chini in most chiya most days, sakhar in chaku, in winter sweets, and in a cup when somebody wants the darker taste.

## Why Does Sakhar Mean Sugar in Marathi?

If you searched for sakhar in English from Maharashtra, your answer is different, and it would be dishonest of us to bury it. In Marathi, साखर (sakhar) is sugar. The ordinary white kind. A Marathi recipe that asks for a cup of sakhar wants the sugar in your tin, and jaggery in Marathi is गूळ (gul).

Gujarati works in a similar way. Sakar there points to sugar, and jaggery is gol.

So here is the part that costs us the sale. If your recipe is Marathi, you do not want our product. Use white sugar, or use gul where the recipe says gul. A Nepali sakhar block swapped in for Marathi sakhar will change the colour, the taste and the way the dish sets, and not in any way the recipe planned for.

Nobody made a mistake here. It is one word that took two roads.

## Where Does the Word Sakhar Come From?

Sakhar, the Marathi sakhar, the Hindi shakkar, the Arabic sukkar and the English word sugar all come from one ancestor, the Sanskrit śarkarā, which meant grit or gravel. Each language kept the word and pointed it at whatever sugar it knew best.

In Marathi it landed on refined sugar. In the Nepali hills it stayed with the solid block that households boiled themselves, because for most of that history there was no other kind.

So an English speaker saying sugar is, in a roundabout way, saying sakhar. The meaning drifted. The sound mostly did not.

## What Is Sakhar Called in Hindi?

In Hindi, the word for jaggery is gur, also written gud (गुड़). If you are Nepali and talking to a Hindi speaker, gur is the word to use. If a Kathmandu shopkeeper calls a block gud, it usually tells you the block came from the Terai or from across the border rather than from the hills.

Hindi also has shakkar (शक्कर), which sounds closest to sakhar. It generally means sugar. In some north Indian kitchens, Punjabi ones in particular, shakkar means a coarse powdered jaggery instead, which is close to what we sell as [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder).

If a Hindi recipe says shakkar and you cannot tell which one it means, look at the photograph of the finished dish. Brown usually means jaggery.

## Sakhar in Nepali, Hindi, Marathi and English: One Table

:::table What jaggery and white sugar are called in each language
Language | Jaggery (unrefined) | White sugar
English | Jaggery | Sugar
Nepali | Sakhar (सख्खर), also gur | Chini (चिनी)
Hindi | Gur, gud (गुड़) | Chini (चीनी), often shakkar (शक्कर)
Marathi | Gul (गूळ) | Sakhar (साखर)
Gujarati | Gol | Sakar
:::

**Where these names come from.** The Nepali column is how we, our cane growers and our customers use the words every day. The category itself, unrefined sugar that keeps its molasses, is described in the [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar) entry and in the [Sugar Tech review of non-centrifugal sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/). Regional usage shifts from one kitchen to the next, so treat the Hindi and Gujarati columns as the usual meaning, not the only one.

## Is Jaggery the Same as Brown Sugar?

Not quite, and the difference matters if you are converting a recipe. Most supermarket brown sugar is refined white sugar with some molasses put back. Jaggery never had its molasses taken off in the first place. It also comes as a hard block rather than loose crystals, unless someone crushes it.

In a recipe, dark brown sugar is the nearest English substitute for sakhar, and muscovado is nearer still. Neither tastes of woodsmoke, which is the part that comes from the fire rather than the cane.

Do not expect much from the difference in your body. Jaggery keeps a trace of the minerals refining strips out, and that trace is small. Per spoon it carries close to the same calories as sugar, and it raises blood glucose the way sugar does. We have put the two side by side in [jaggery vs sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar), and gone through [the benefits people claim for sakhar](/blog/jaggery-health-claims-truth) one at a time. If you have diabetes, read [our honest answer on jaggery and diabetes](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics), and ask your doctor rather than a shop.

## Why Do People Call It Sankhuwasabha Sakhar?

In Nepal, hill sakhar is usually asked for by the place it comes from. Ours is made on terraces in Sankhuwasabha, in the Koshi hills, and the people who buy it ask for Sankhuwasabha sakhar, or just Sankhuwa sakhar. The place in the name does real work. It tells you the block was boiled in the hills, over wood, in small batches, rather than made at scale on the plains.

The cane for our current batches was cut in Mangsir. The fire goes on before light, the foam is skimmed by hand for as long as it keeps rising, and the blocks set overnight in the open air. The longer version, including where Terai gur is the better buy, is in [what Sankhuwasabha sakhar is and why it differs](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha).

If you want to be sure the block in your hand is sakhar and not sugar boiled into a block shape, the [seven home tests for pure sakhar](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) are worth ten minutes of your time.

![Sakhar in English is jaggery: a dark hand-poured Nepali sakhar block beside a bowl of white sugar](/blog/sakhar-in-english/sakhar-in-english-jaggery-vs-sugar.jpg "Both of these are called sakhar somewhere. In Nepal, it is the one on the left.")

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is jaggery called in Nepali?

Jaggery in Nepali is sakhar (सख्खर), also spelled sakhkhar. In the Terai it is often called gur or gud (गुड़). White sugar is chini (चिनी).

### What is sakhar called in English?

In Nepali, sakhar is jaggery, the unrefined cane sugar sold as a hard brown block or a powder. In Marathi, sakhar means white sugar. So the English word depends on which language the word sakhar came from.

### What is sakhar in Hindi?

The Hindi word for jaggery is gur, also written gud (गुड़). Shakkar (शक्कर) sounds closer to sakhar but usually means sugar, although in some Punjabi kitchens it means powdered jaggery.

### Is sakhar sugar or jaggery?

Both, depending on the language. In Nepali, sakhar is jaggery and white sugar is chini. In Marathi, sakhar is white sugar and jaggery is gul.

### Is jaggery the same as brown sugar?

No. Most brown sugar is refined sugar with molasses added back. Jaggery is cane juice boiled down with its molasses never removed, and it is usually sold as a solid block. Dark brown sugar or muscovado is the closest swap in a recipe.

### Is sakhar healthier than sugar?

Only slightly. It keeps a small trace of minerals and is made without bleaching agents, but it is still sugar, with similar calories and a similar effect on blood glucose. The [WHO guideline on sugars intake](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028) applies to it in full.

### How do you spell sakhar?

In Nepali it is सख्खर, romanised as sakhar or sakhkhar, and sometimes written सखर. The Marathi word, which means sugar, is साखर.

### What is the difference between sakhar and chaku?

Sakhar is the plain jaggery block. Chaku is a sweet made from it, cooked with ghee and often sesame, and eaten at Maghe Sankranti. We make sakhar, not chaku, and our [chaku guide](/blog/chaku-recipe-maghe-sankranti) shows how to make it at home.

## So What Is Sakhar in English?

If the word came from Nepal, sakhar is jaggery, and the closest English kitchen swap is dark brown sugar. If it came from Maharashtra, sakhar is sugar, and you should use sugar. That is the whole translation.

If it is the Nepali one you are after, this is [our sakhar block from Sankhuwasabha](/products/organic-jaggery-block), and the same batch [crushed to a powder](/products/jaggery-powder) if you sweeten a cup every day. You can read [who makes it and where](/our-story).

Use less of it than you think. It is still sugar, whatever the word.

title: Jaggery Powder vs Block: Which Sakhar Should You Buy?
seoTitle: Jaggery Powder vs Block: Which Sakhar to Buy
description: Our powder is our block, crushed. Jaggery powder vs block on price, dissolving, taste and shelf life, and which one your kitchen actually wants.
content:
The question arrives most weeks, usually by message, usually with a photograph attached: a resealable pouch in one hand and a dense amber disc in the other, and underneath it, which one is better?

It is a fair question and the answer disappoints people slightly. Neither. When you compare jaggery powder vs block, you are not comparing two grades of sakhar. You are comparing one sakhar in two shapes, and the right one depends entirely on what happens to it in your kitchen.

We make sakhar (सख्खर, also spelled sakhkhar), or jaggery, over a wood fire on terraces in [Sankhuwasabha](/our-story), and we make both. The powder is the block. So here is the honest version of the comparison, including the case for buying the cheaper one and the case for buying neither.

> They are the same sakhar. Our powder is our block, crushed and sieved, with nothing added. Buy the block if you cook with it, get through a kilo, or want the lowest price by weight. Buy the powder if you sweeten a cup daily, bake, or need something that dissolves cold. Quality is not the variable here.

![Jaggery powder vs block: Nepali sakhar powder in a pouch beside a hand-poured disc](/blog/jaggery-powder-vs-block/jaggery-powder-vs-block-nepal.jpg "Same kadhai, same fire, same day. One of them went through a sieve.")

## Are Sakhar Powder and Block the Same Sakhar?

Yes, and in our case that is not a figure of speech. The [Sakhar Powder](/products/jaggery-powder) is made from the [Sakhar Block](/products/organic-jaggery-block), after the block has fully set. It is crushed, sieved to an even grain, and packed straight into a sealed pouch.

Nothing is added at that step. No anti-caking agent, no starch, no flour, no sugar to bulk it out. If you bought a kilo of our block and put it through a grinder at home, you would have our powder, minus the sieving and minus the seal.

This is true of the category generally. Unrefined cane sugar is sold as blocks, cones, granules and syrup across South Asia and Latin America, and all of it is [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar) made the same way: press the juice, boil it down, let it set. The shape is a decision taken at the end. It is packing, not recipe.

This matters because powdered jaggery is where adulteration is easiest to hide. A block shows you its own grain, colour and set. A powder has been through a machine already, and anything mixed into it disappears. That is a general warning about powdered jaggery, ours included, and it is why the tests in [how to identify pure jaggery](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) are easier to run on a block than on a pouch.

So the first honest thing to say is that the powder asks for more trust than the block does. Buy it from someone who will tell you what is in it.

## Jaggery Powder vs Block: The Comparison in One Table

:::table Our two forms of the same sakhar, side by side
 | Sakhar Block | Sakhar Powder
Pack | 1kg, about three hand-poured discs | 250g resealable pouch
Price | Rs. 400 | Rs. 149
Price per kg | Rs. 400 | About Rs. 596
Stated shelf life | 6 to 12 months | 6 months
Dissolves in a cold drink | No | Yes
Needs chipping or grating | Yes | No
Measures like sugar | No | Yes
Best for | Cooking, chaku, households getting through a kilo | Daily chiya, baking, anyone who wants no extra step
:::

**Where these numbers come from.** The prices, pack sizes and shelf lives are the ones on our own [block](/products/organic-jaggery-block) and [powder](/products/jaggery-powder) product pages. The per-kilo figure for the powder is arithmetic on our own pack, worked through properly in [what sakhar costs in Nepal](/sakhar-price). The shelf lives are based on how our sakhar behaves in storage rather than on laboratory testing, which we have not had done, and both assume the storage described in [how to store sakhar](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar).

## Which One Dissolves Better?

The powder, comfortably, and this is the single most practical difference between them.

Crushing the block multiplies its surface area, and dissolving is a surface event. Powder disperses on contact in anything hot and will go into a cold drink as well, which the block simply will not do. A disc dropped into cold lassi or cold milk sits there.

The block dissolves perfectly well in hot liquid, but on its own schedule and only if you help it. Grate it on the fine side of a grater first. A lump of anything dropped whole into a pan takes a minute of stirring, and in a milk chiya that minute is exactly when [the milk splits](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling).

If your entire use for sakhar is one cup of chiya in the morning, this difference is most of the decision.

## Does the Block Taste Different from the Powder?

Slightly, and in a direction most people do not expect.

The block tastes stronger. Toasted molasses lands first and there is a long mineral finish behind it, carrying a faint smoke from the wood fire the juice was reduced over. It chips rather than crumbles, and a chip eaten on its own is the reference flavour of everything we make.

The powder reads lighter. Crushing exposes far more surface to the air, which softens that smoke and pushes a cleaner caramel forward. Nothing was removed. It simply presents differently once it is in pieces.

Which one is nicer is a matter of taste and not of quality. People who like sakhar for its smoke tend to prefer the block. People who want a drop-in replacement for sugar tend to prefer the powder, because the powder gets out of the way.

Worth saying plainly: composition varies between blocks anyway, with cane, soil, season and how long the kadhai ran, which is documented in the [review of non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/). Two of our own blocks poured a month apart are not identical either.

## Which Works Out Cheaper?

The block, by a clear margin, and it is not close.

Our block is Rs. 400 a kilo. Our powder is Rs. 149 for 250g, which is about Rs. 596 a kilo. You are paying roughly half as much again by weight for the same sakhar in a different shape.

What that premium buys is a processing step and a smaller, sealed pack. Both are real costs on our side and both are real conveniences on yours. What it does not buy is a better product, and we would rather write that down than let anyone assume the more expensive pouch is the superior one.

If you cook with sakhar, or get through a kilo in a month, buy the block and keep a grater next to it. The full argument about what sakhar should cost, including when someone else's cheaper gur is the sensible buy, is in [sakhar price in Nepal](/sakhar-price).

## Which One Keeps Longer?

The block, again, and for a reason that follows from the same physics as the dissolving.

We sell the block as six to twelve months and the powder as six. All that surface area which makes powder dissolve so well also makes it pull moisture out of the air faster, so an opened pouch left loose in a Kathmandu monsoon will cake into a solid lump long before a block goes tacky.

Caked powder is not spoiled. Break it up with a fork and it behaves exactly as it did. But it is the form that punishes a bad container, so decant it into a small airtight jar and use a dry spoon. Both forms want the same treatment, set out in [how to store sakhar](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar).

If you are buying ahead, or buying several kilos before the season ends, buy blocks. They are the more patient form.

## Which Should You Use for Baking and Cooking?

Powder for baking, block for anything that melts.

In a batter or a dough, you need something that creams and distributes, and a grated block is a poor substitute for a genuine even grain. Our powder swaps one for one where a recipe asks for brown sugar. Against white sugar, start at about three quarters of the amount, because sakhar reads sweeter and browns faster, and check the bake early.

For anything with a melting step, the block is better and cheaper. Syrups, kheer, halwa, and [chaku for Maghe Sankranti](/blog/chaku-recipe-maghe-sankranti) all start by melting sakhar down with a little water, and a block does that as well as a powder does at two thirds the price by weight.

Neither form suits meringue, pale cakes or a clear syrup. Both will take those brown and cloudy, which is covered along with the rest of the swap in [sakhar against white sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar). Keep the white packet for those and use it without guilt.

## So Which One Should You Buy?

:::compare
You sweeten one or two cups of chiya a day and nothing else | The powder. It dissolves without thought, measures like sugar, and a 250g pouch is a sensible amount to get through before it needs babying. This is the largest group of people asking the question.
You cook, bake in quantity, or make festival sweets | The block, and a grater. You will use the price difference, and the melting step makes the extra work disappear.
You want to taste what hill sakhar actually is | The block. It is the reference flavour, and a chip of it eaten on its own is the honest introduction.
You are buying it as a gift | The block. It looks like what it is, hand-poured and uneven, and it survives being carried around.
You have never bought sakhar before | The powder, once, as the cheaper mistake to make. If you like it, move to the block.
You are stocking up for months | Blocks. They keep longer and cost less by weight.
:::

## When You Should Buy Neither

The part our accountant would cut.

If you sweeten a cup occasionally and are not particular about where it came from, a Terai gur block from your local shop will do the job at a fraction of what we charge, and it is a good product made by people who know what they are doing. We argue that hill sakhar tastes different and is worth the premium to some people, and we set out where that difference is smaller than we would like in [what makes hill sakhar different](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha). It is a preference, not an upgrade everyone needs to buy.

And if you are choosing between powder and block because you have read that jaggery is good for you, stop and read [what sakhar actually does](/blog/jaggery-health-claims-truth) first. Both forms are sugar. The [WHO suggests keeping free sugars under about 25 grams a day](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children), and sakhar counts inside that in whichever shape it arrives. Choosing the healthier of two identical sugars is not a decision that exists.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is jaggery powder better than jaggery block?

No. In our case the powder is the block crushed and sieved, with nothing added, so neither is a better grade. The powder is more convenient and costs more by weight. The block is cheaper, keeps longer and has a slightly stronger flavour.

### Why is jaggery powder more expensive than the block?

Because it is the block plus a processing step and a smaller, sealed pack. Ours is Rs. 149 for 250g, about Rs. 596 a kilo, against Rs. 400 a kilo for the block. You are paying for convenience rather than for a different sakhar.

### Can I make jaggery powder at home from a block?

Yes. Break a set block up and grind it in a mixer in short pulses, then sieve it. It will not be as even as a sieved commercial grain and it starts pulling in moisture immediately, so make a little at a time and keep it in a sealed jar.

### Which jaggery is best for tea?

Powder, for most people, because it dissolves on contact and never sits as a lump in hot milk. A grated block works equally well. What causes curdling is the order you add things in rather than the form of the sakhar.

### Does jaggery powder dissolve in cold water?

Yes, which is the one thing the block genuinely cannot do. Powder will go into cold milk, lassi or a cold drink. A piece of block will sit at the bottom of the glass.

### Which form of jaggery lasts longer?

The block. We sell it as six to twelve months against six for the powder. Powder has far more surface area, so it draws in humidity and cakes faster, especially through the monsoon.

### Is powdered jaggery more likely to be adulterated?

As a category, yes, and that applies to everyone selling it. A block shows you its grain, colour and set, while anything mixed into a powder is invisible. Buy powder from a seller who states what is in it, and run the home tests on a block where you can.

### Should I buy the 1kg block if there are only two of us?

Usually yes, if you cook with it at all. A kilo is about three discs, it keeps six to twelve months stored properly, and it works out a third cheaper by weight. Break it up once and keep the pieces in a jar.

## The Verdict on Jaggery Powder vs Block

Buy the block unless convenience is the thing you actually want, in which case buy the powder and do not feel talked out of it. Both are the same sakhar off the same fire, and the only real variables are price, dissolving and how much handling you are prepared to do.

Most households that cook end up with both: a [1kg block](/products/organic-jaggery-block) in a jar for cooking and melting, and a [250g pouch](/products/jaggery-powder) beside the kettle for chiya. That is what we keep in our own kitchen, and it is not a sales line, it is just what the two forms are good at.

Whichever you pick, use less of it than you want to. That advice has never once helped us sell more sakhar and we keep printing it anyway.

My father grates the block. My mother keeps the pouch. They have been sweetening the same pot of chiya for thirty years and have never resolved it.

title: How to Store Sakhar So It Does Not Go Sticky or Mouldy
seoTitle: How to Store Jaggery So It Does Not Go Sticky
description: Sakhar goes sticky because it pulls water out of the air, not because it has spoiled. How to store jaggery in a Nepali kitchen, and when to bin a block.
content:
The jar on the windowsill is always the one that goes first. Ours did, that first year in the Kapan kitchen: a kilo block that came off the hill in Mangsir hard enough to knock against the counter, and by the end of the monsoon soft enough to hold the print of a thumb.

Most people decide the sakhar has spoiled, or that they were sold something adulterated. Usually it is neither, and knowing how to store jaggery is the whole difference.

It is the block doing what an unrefined block does in a wet Kathmandu August, and the fix is a container, not a refund.

We make sakhar (सख्खर, also spelled sakhkhar), or jaggery, over a wood fire on terraces in [Sankhuwasabha](/our-story), and we get asked about this more than almost anything else. So here is the method that works, what a softening block is actually telling you, and the point at which one is genuinely finished.

> Keep sakhar airtight, dark, cool and away from steam. Glass or steel with a tight lid beats the bag it arrived in. Sakhar softens because it pulls water from the air, not because it has gone off, so a sticky block is usually still good. Throw it out for fuzzy mould or a fermented smell.

![A block of Nepali sakhar stored in a sealed glass jar in a dark kitchen cupboard](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar-nepal.jpg "One kilo, broken down, in glass with a real seal. This is the whole method.")

## Why Does Sakhar Go Sticky?

Sakhar is hygroscopic, which is a long word for a simple habit: it takes water out of the air around it and holds on to it.

Refined white chini has been stripped down to sucrose crystals and very little else. Sakhar has not. Boiling cane juice down and pouring it to set leaves the molasses in, and with it the glucose and fructose that refining removes, along with minerals and the cane's own organic acids. That published [review of non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) sets out how much the composition varies between one block and the next depending on cane, soil and method.

Those retained sugars are the sticky part. They attract moisture far more readily than plain sucrose does, so a block left open in a humid room slowly draws water into its surface and turns tacky. Nothing has rotted. The block has simply got wetter.

### The monsoon is the whole problem in Nepal

From June to September, a Nepali kitchen is a humid room with a stove in it. Rice steams, pressure cookers vent, and the air does not dry out between meals.

That is the season when the questions arrive, and it is why an unopened block bought in Mangsir can sit happily until Asar and then soften in a fortnight. It is also why the same block in the same jar behaves impeccably all winter. We have never measured the humidity in our own store room, so treat that as observation rather than data.

## What a Softening Block Is Actually Telling You

Here is the part our sales figures would prefer we left out.

A block of sakhar that softens in the monsoon is behaving the way honestly made jaggery behaves. A block that stays glassy, uniformly golden and rock hard through a Kathmandu August, month after month, is worth a harder look. Blocks get treated to hold their colour and their set, which is one of the things the home tests in [how to identify pure jaggery](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) are looking for.

So yes: ours will go soft on you if you leave it out, and we are not going to pretend that is a defect in someone else's product and a feature in ours. It is the same chemistry either way. Good storage is what stands between you and it.

## How to Store Jaggery: The Method That Works

Six steps, none of which need anything you do not already own.

1. Make sure the block is dry and at room temperature before it goes away. A piece that has been near steam, or cut with a wet knife, carries that water into the jar with it.
2. Use a rigid, genuinely airtight container. Glass with a rubber gasket, or steel with a clamp lid. The polythene the block travelled in is not a storage container and never was.
3. Break the kilo down before you store it, not each time you need some. Every opening lets a lungful of wet air in, and a jar opened twice a day is a jar you are ventilating.
4. Keep it dark and cool. The back of a cupboard, not the shelf above the gas, not the windowsill, not the counter beside the kettle.
5. Store it away from anything strongly scented. Sakhar takes on the smell of masala, kerosene and soap given long enough, and it does not give them back.
6. Keep powder and block in separate jars. They behave differently, and the powder is the one that will clump first.

If you buy a kilo at a time, that is genuinely all of it. The single highest-value change most kitchens can make is the second one, moving the block out of its bag and into glass.

## Cupboard, Fridge or Freezer: Where Should Sakhar Live?

:::compare
A cool dark cupboard | The right answer nearly always, and the only one that needs no thought. Airtight jar, back of the shelf, away from the stove. This is where ours lives.
The fridge | Defensible in the worst of the monsoon, with one catch that undoes most people. Cold sakhar pulls condensation the moment it meets warm kitchen air, so it must come out sealed and be left to reach room temperature before the lid comes off. Open it cold and you have watered it yourself.
The freezer | Works, and is more trouble than it is worth for a sweetener you reach for daily. Reasonable if you have bought several kilos and want to hold some back for months. Same rule as the fridge, doubled: seal it, thaw it sealed, and only then open it.
:::

For a household getting through a kilo in a month or two, the cupboard wins on every count. The fridge is a monsoon tactic, not a default.

## How Long Does Sakhar Keep?

Longer than most people expect, because sugar at this concentration is a poor place for anything to grow. What actually ends a block is moisture, and moisture is the thing you control.

:::table What we put on our own packs
Product | Stated shelf life | The condition that matters
[Sakhar Block, 1kg](/products/organic-jaggery-block) | 6 to 12 months | A cool, dry place
[Sakhar Powder, 250g](/products/jaggery-powder) | 6 months | An airtight container
:::

**Where these numbers come from.** They are the figures we print on our own packaging and publish on the product pages, based on how our blocks behave in storage rather than on laboratory testing, which we have not had done. The wider point that composition and moisture vary between blocks is documented in the [Sugar Tech review of non-centrifugal sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) and in the general description of [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar). If we ever put a batch through a lab, we will publish what comes back, including the parts we do not like.

Both figures assume the storage above. A block left open on a counter through August can go tacky in weeks, and a sealed jar in a dark cupboard will comfortably outlast the date.

## Mould, Bloom or Crystals: What Is Growing on My Sakhar?

Four things turn up on a stored block, and only two of them mean it is over.

:::compare
A fine white powdery bloom | Sugar crystallising out at the surface as moisture moves. Harmless. Brush it off or ignore it, and check your seal.
Sticky syrup pooling at the bottom | Drawn moisture, exactly as described above. The block is wetter than it was. If it smells like sakhar, use it.
Grey, green, blue or black fuzz | Mould. It needed the moisture you let in. Do not scrape it off and keep the rest, and do not argue with it. The block is finished.
A sour, yeasty or alcoholic smell | Fermentation, meaning there was enough water for yeasts to work. Finished as well, and it will taste like it.
:::

We are jaggery producers, not a food safety authority. The honest rule is the boring one every kitchen already knows: if you are standing there wondering whether it is fine, it is not worth the Rs. 400. Throw it out.

## Storing Sakhar Powder Is a Different Job

Powder is the same sakhar with vastly more surface area, so everything above happens to it faster. It does not soften into a tacky mass so much as clump into a single brick in the corner of the pouch.

The pouch it comes in is fine sealed and poor once opened. Decant it into a small airtight jar, keep the jar somewhere dark, and use a properly dry spoon every time. A damp teaspoon going back into the powder is how most jars set solid.

If it has already clumped, it has not spoiled. Break it up with the back of a spoon and it dissolves as it always did, which is one of the reasons [powder is the easier form for chiya](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling).

## Can You Rescue a Block That Has Gone Soft?

Usually, yes, as long as it smells right and nothing is growing on it.

Move it to a proper airtight jar and leave it somewhere dark and dry for a few days. It will firm up as the surface moisture equalises. It will not go back to being the hard dry block it was in Mangsir, and it does not need to.

Failing that, use it where texture is irrelevant, which is most places. Softened sakhar grates easily, dissolves faster in chiya than a hard block does, and melts down perfectly well for [chaku at Maghe Sankranti](/blog/chaku-recipe-maghe-sankranti). A block that has lost its snap has lost nothing that matters in a pan.

## Does Where the Sakhar Was Made Change How It Keeps?

Somewhat, and less than the marketing suggests.

Hill sakhar and Terai gur are made by the same method with different cane and different weather, and how a block sets depends on how far the juice was reduced and how humid the day was when it was poured. A drier, harder block starts further from the point at which it goes tacky. That is a head start, not immunity, and we go into what does and does not differ in [what makes hill sakhar different](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha).

What matters more than provenance is what happened after you carried it home. A superb block in an open bag on a windowsill will be sticky before a mediocre one in a sealed jar in a cupboard.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do you store jaggery long term?

Airtight, dark, cool and dry. A glass or steel container with a real seal, kept at the back of a cupboard away from the stove and any window. Break a large block into usable pieces first so you are not opening the container every day.

### Does jaggery need to be refrigerated?

No, and for most of the year it is better off out of the fridge. A cool dark cupboard in an airtight jar is enough. In the worst of the monsoon the fridge is reasonable, provided the container stays sealed until it has come back to room temperature.

### Why has my jaggery gone sticky?

It has absorbed moisture from the air. Sakhar keeps the molasses that refining strips out of white sugar, and those sugars attract water. It is a storage problem, not spoilage, and a sealed jar in a dry cupboard usually reverses it.

### Can you eat jaggery with white mould on it?

No. White fuzzy growth is mould and the block should go. A fine dry powdery bloom is different, that is sugar crystallising at the surface and is harmless. Fuzz is fuzz. If you are unsure, throw it out.

### How long does jaggery last once opened?

Our blocks are sold as six to twelve months and the powder as six, kept as described above. Opened and stored well, that holds. Opened and left in its bag through a monsoon, it can go tacky within weeks, though tacky is not the same as inedible.

### Does jaggery expire or go bad?

It does not expire the way fresh food does, because very little grows in something this concentrated. What ends a block is moisture: enough of it and you get mould or fermentation, and at that point it is over. Kept dry, sakhar is one of the more forgiving things in a kitchen.

### Should jaggery be stored in the same jar as jaggery powder?

Better not to. They take on moisture at different rates, and the powder clumps long before the block softens. Two small jars keep each one at its best and stop you opening the block every time you want a spoon of powder.

### Is it safe to keep jaggery near spices?

Only if both are properly sealed. Sakhar picks up strong smells over weeks and does not release them, so a jar sitting open beside masala or soap will eventually taste of it.

## So, How Should You Store Sakhar?

In glass, in the dark, sealed, broken into pieces, nowhere near the stove. That is the entire answer, and it costs one jar.

The rest is a matter of expectations. Sakhar is unrefined, which is the reason to buy it and also the reason it behaves like this. It softens in the wet months, it firms up in the dry ones, and a block that never moves at all through a Nepali monsoon is telling you something about itself. What ends a block is mould or a fermented smell, and almost nothing else.

If you are starting a fresh kilo, the [1kg block](/products/organic-jaggery-block) is the one worth breaking down into a jar on the day it arrives. The [250g powder](/products/jaggery-powder) is easier still, provided it comes out of its pouch.

And the same thing we say at the end of everything here, storage or not: whichever jar it is in, eat less of it than you want to. The [WHO suggests keeping free sugars under about 25 grams a day](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children), and sakhar counts inside that limit exactly as chini does. A well-stored kilo should last you a good while. If it is not lasting, that is worth noticing too.

My grandmother kept hers in a steel dabba with a lid that had to be worked loose with a thumbnail, on the darkest shelf in the house, and I never once saw a block of it go bad.

The cane comes off the terraces her family and forty-one neighbouring households farm in Sankhuwasabha, the way they have made sakhar for seven generations.

title: Jaggery Benefits: What Sakhar Actually Does, and What It Does Not
seoTitle: Jaggery Benefits: What Is True and What Is Not
description: Jaggery benefits, checked by the people who make sakhar: twelve health claims, from anaemia to weight loss, and which are true, traditional or false.
content:
A shop in Kathmandu last winter had a hand-written card propped against a tray of gur. It said the jaggery on that tray was good for anaemia, good for the lungs, good for the skin and good for losing weight. The woman selling it was not lying to anybody. She had read the same claims we have all read, on packaging and in listings and from her own supplier, and she was passing them on.

We make and sell sakhar (सख्खर, also spelled sakhkhar, and called gur in much of Nepal). So when we say most of what is written about jaggery benefits, sakhar benefits included, is not true, understand that we are arguing against our own marketing.

> Sakhar is unrefined sugar. It keeps a trace of the minerals refining strips out, it is made without bleaching agents or chemical clarifiers, and it tastes better than white sugar in chiya. That is the whole honest case for it. It does not detox anything, it does not cure anaemia, it will not help you lose weight, and it is not a medicine.

## Where These Claims Come From

Very few of them are invented from nothing. Most are a traditional use that hardened into a health claim somewhere between a grandmother and a product label.

Jaggery has been part of Nepali and South Asian food for a very long time, and traditional food systems assign meanings to foods that are about warmth, season and occasion rather than about pharmacology. Those meanings are real and worth respecting. They are not the same as evidence, and the trouble starts when a label prints them as though they were.

This is a habit across our whole industry, and we have to resist it ourselves. It is genuinely tempting to let a warm sentence stand because it sells. The reason we do not is that a customer who believes sakhar will fix their anaemia is a customer we have actively misled, and no amount of good jaggery makes up for that.

## What Sakhar Does Not Do

Each of these is a claim we have seen printed. The verdict is ours, and the reasoning is short on purpose.

### Does sakhar detox the liver?

**No good evidence.** There is no recognised process by which a sweetener assists the liver. A healthy liver is not waiting for help from food, and a damaged one needs a doctor. "Detox" is a marketing word rather than a physiological one.

### Does sakhar help you lose weight?

**No good evidence, and the claim runs the wrong way.** Sakhar is sugar and it is energy-dense. Swapping white sugar for sakhar changes almost nothing about the calories going in. If somebody loses weight after switching, the likely reason is that they started paying attention to sugar at all, which they could have done without buying anything from us.

### Does sakhar prevent asthma?

**No good evidence.** This one is worth naming directly because believing it could delay someone getting treatment for a condition that is genuinely dangerous. Asthma is managed medically. Nothing on a jaggery label belongs in that conversation.

### Is sakhar antiseptic?

**No good evidence.** Concentrated sugar solutions do inhibit some microbial growth, which is why jam keeps, and that fact has been stretched into a claim about what happens inside a person. Those are not the same thing.

### Is sakhar good for your skin?

**No good evidence.** Sugar scrubs exist and jaggery is sometimes used in them, but that is an abrasive being used as an abrasive. Eating sakhar does not improve skin, and eating a lot of any sugar is more plausibly the opposite.

### Does sakhar boost immunity?

**No good evidence.** "Immunity" claims are almost never specific enough to test, which is exactly why they appear on so much packaging. We would want to know boosts what, measured how, before repeating it.

## What Is Traditional Rather Than Proven

These are different. Naming them as tradition is not the same as calling them false, and we would rather be precise than dismissive.

### Does sakhar help digestion or relieve constipation?

**Traditional.** Sakhar after a meal is a long-standing practice across the region. We are not aware of good evidence that it does anything mechanical for digestion. If it settles the end of a meal for you, that is a real experience and a reasonable enough reason to eat a little.

### Does sakhar ease period pain?

**Traditional.** Warm sweet drinks are a widespread comfort during menstruation and comfort has value. There is no good evidence that jaggery specifically relieves cramps. Anyone whose period pain is severe or worsening should see a doctor rather than adjust a sweetener.

### Is sakhar good for a cold or a cough?

**Traditional, and the mechanism is probably the drink.** Warm liquid soothes a sore throat, and sakhar in hot water with ginger is a comfort a great many Nepali households make. That is the warmth and the fluid doing the work. It is a nice thing to drink when you feel awful. It is not a treatment.

## The Two That Belong With a Doctor

This section is general information about food, not medical advice. If either of these applies to you, please take it to a doctor, a midwife or a nurse rather than to a jaggery producer. We are producers, and it would be wrong of us to pretend otherwise.

### Is sakhar a good source of iron?

**No, and this is the claim we would most like to see disappear.** Sakhar does keep a small mineral fraction that refined sugar loses, iron included, and we say so ourselves in [sakhar and sugar, honestly](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar). But we also say the part the labels leave out: you would have to eat a genuinely harmful quantity of sakhar to get a useful amount of iron out of it. Treat the minerals as a small bonus, never as a reason to eat more.

### Does sakhar cure or prevent anaemia?

**No.** This one deserves care, because people searching it are often worried and are often acting on advice from family who love them. The tradition of giving jaggery to someone who is weak or recovering is kind and it comes from a good place.

Anaemia is a medical condition. It is diagnosed with a blood test and treated with supplements or, in some cases, infusions, under medical supervision. Relying on a sweetener instead of that is the one scenario where believing a jaggery claim can genuinely cost someone their health. If you or someone in your family is being treated for anaemia, sakhar is food, not part of the treatment.

### Is sakhar safe in pregnancy?

**It is food, and the same rules apply as to any sugar.** There is nothing about sakhar that makes it dangerous in pregnancy in ordinary amounts, and nothing that makes it beneficial either. What matters is total sugar, and gestational diabetes and blood sugar in pregnancy are questions for a doctor or midwife who knows the person in front of them. We have written the whole question up in [jaggery in pregnancy](/blog/jaggery-in-pregnancy), including iron, the hot food belief and sakhar in sutkeri after the birth. Our article on [whether sakhar is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics) covers the blood sugar question properly, and it also ends by telling people to ask a clinician.

## So How Much Is Reasonable?

The World Health Organization suggests adults keep free sugars [below about 25 grams a day](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children), with the full reasoning in its [guideline on sugars intake](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028). Sakhar is a free sugar and counts towards that in full. Unrefined does not mean uncounted.

That is roughly four or five cups of sweetened chiya before anything else sweet in the day, which is less than it sounds when there is a tray of sweets in the house.

## What Are the Real Benefits of Jaggery?

Having spent two thousand words taking things away, here is what is left, and it is not nothing.

Sakhar is **unrefined**. It is not spun in a centrifuge and stripped back to sucrose, which is the process refined sugar exists at the end of. The [review literature on non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) describes a product that retains a mineral and phenolic fraction refined sugar does not have, and the [USDA entry for granulated sugar](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/portal-data/external/169655) shows what is left when you take that away, which is essentially sucrose and nothing else. That difference is real. It is also small, per spoon, which is why we will not build a health claim on it.

Sakhar made properly is **made without additives**. No sulphur, no chemical clarifier, no bleaching agent, no colour. That is a description of a method rather than a certification, and it is the thing worth checking, which is why we published [seven ways to tell pure sakhar from adulterated](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar) and a [test you can run in your kitchen](/tools/sakhar-purity-test).

Sakhar is **traceable**. A good block comes from one field and one fire, and ours comes from [terraces in Sankhuwasabha](/our-story) that we can name. Almost nothing else on a sugar shelf can say that. If you want to know what that produces, it is the [1kg block](/products/organic-jaggery-block), or the [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) if you would rather not chip at one, and there is more on what hill sakhar actually is in [Himalayan jaggery](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha).

And it tastes better. In chiya, in chaku, over curd, it tastes of boiled cane and woodsmoke instead of tasting of nothing. That is a good reason to buy sakhar. It is a better reason than any of the twelve claims above, and it has the advantage of being true.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does jaggery detox the liver?

No. There is no good evidence that any sweetener assists liver function, and "detox" is a marketing term rather than a physiological process. A healthy liver does not need help from food.

### Is jaggery good for anaemia?

No. Jaggery keeps a trace of iron that refined sugar loses, but not in a quantity that treats anaemia. Anaemia is diagnosed by blood test and treated medically. Please see a doctor rather than relying on a sweetener.

### Does jaggery help you lose weight?

No. Jaggery is sugar and is energy-dense. Replacing white sugar with jaggery does not meaningfully change the calories you eat. Using less of either is what makes the difference.

### Is jaggery safe during pregnancy?

In ordinary amounts it is food like any other sugar, and it counts towards your total sugar. Blood sugar in pregnancy and gestational diabetes are medical questions. Ask a doctor or midwife who knows your situation. The longer answer is in [jaggery in pregnancy](/blog/jaggery-in-pregnancy).

### Does jaggery help period pain?

There is no good evidence that it does. Warm sweet drinks are a traditional comfort and comfort is worth something, but severe or worsening period pain should be seen by a doctor.

### Is jaggery good for a cold?

Warm liquid soothes a sore throat, so sakhar in hot water with ginger genuinely feels good when you are ill. That is the warm drink rather than the jaggery. It is not a treatment for an infection.

### Does jaggery boost immunity?

There is no good evidence for this, and the claim is rarely specific enough to test. We would want to know what is being boosted, and measured how, before repeating it.

### Is jaggery good for health?

In small amounts it is a slightly better sugar than refined white sugar, because it is unrefined and made without chemicals. It is still a sugar, and it is not a superfood. Anyone selling it as one, ourselves included, should be asked what they mean.

## Before You Believe the Next Label

The test we would suggest is simple. When a jaggery label makes a health claim, ask what it would take to prove it, and ask whether the seller has done that. Almost nobody has, us included.

What a seller can honestly tell you is where the cane grew, what fuel the fire burned, what went into the pan and what did not, and when the batch was made. Those are checkable, and a seller who answers them precisely is telling you more than one who promises your skin will improve.

Eat less sugar than you currently do. That includes ours.

title: How to Identify Pure Sakhar: 7 Simple Tests You Can Do at Home
seoTitle: How to Identify Pure Sakhar (Jaggery): 7 Home Tests
description: Not sure if your sakhar is pure? Here are 7 jaggery tests you can do at home with water, iodine and your own hands, plus what real hill jaggery looks like.
content:
You bought a block of sakhar (jaggery) that looked perfect in the shop: smooth, golden, shiny. Then you put it in your tea and something was off. A salty edge, a strange smell, or a chalky bit sitting in the bottom of the cup.

If that has happened to you, you are not imagining things. Sakhar is one of the most commonly adulterated sweeteners in South Asia. Most of us buy it loose, by weight, with no label to read.

So here is how to identify pure jaggery at home. No laboratory. Just a glass of warm water, a few drops of iodine and your own hands: seven tests you can finish tonight, with the sakhar already sitting in your kitchen.

> To check if sakhar (jaggery) is pure, dissolve a piece in a glass of warm water. Pure jaggery dissolves fully and leaves no sediment, while adulterated jaggery leaves chalky residue at the bottom. Pure sakhar is also dark brown rather than bright yellow, and it tastes clean and sweet with no salty or bitter aftertaste.

1. [The water test](#test-1-the-water-test)
2. [The colour test](#test-2-the-colour-test)
3. [The taste test](#test-3-the-taste-test)
4. [The iodine test for starch](#test-4-the-iodine-test-for-starch)
5. [The hardness test](#test-5-the-hardness-test)
6. [The rub test](#test-6-the-rub-test)
7. [The smell test](#test-7-the-smell-test)

## What Gets Added to Sakhar, and Why

Before the tests, it helps to know what you are looking for. Four things are commonly added to jaggery, each for a reason.

**Chemical clarifiers.** When cane juice boils, a dark scum rises. Some producers add chemicals such as sulphur or washing soda to strip that scum away, because a paler batch sells faster.

**Artificial colour.** Buyers have been taught that golden jaggery is good jaggery. So dye is used to hit that shade. Sometimes it is metanil yellow, an industrial colour that is not food grade.

**Sugar syrup.** Refined sugar is cheaper than cane juice. Adding it bulks up the batch, adds weight, and makes the block harder and glassier so it survives transport.

**Chalk powder and washing soda.** These are pure weight. A few hundred grams of chalk in a sack of sakhar costs nothing and sells for full price.

None of it is done to help you. It is done for weight, for appearance and for shelf life.

Food safety authorities treat adulteration as an offence, and in Nepal the [Department of Food Technology and Quality Control](http://www.dftqc.gov.np/en/) regulates it. But loose, unlabelled sakhar sold by weight is very hard to police, so the checking has to happen in your kitchen.

If you want to see the other side of it, this is [how we boil our sakhar with nothing added](/our-story).

## Pure Sakhar Test at Home: What You Need First

Almost nothing. A clear glass, warm water, a spoon, a small bottle of tincture of iodine from any pharmacy, and clean hands. Do it near a window, where daylight tells you more than a yellow bulb.

Take two pieces if you can: the sakhar you are suspicious of, and any sample you trust. Testing side by side tells you far more than testing alone.

### One jaggery adulteration test is not enough

No single test is proof. Real sakhar varies: colour changes with the cane, the season and the fire. Run at least three of the seven tests before you decide, and trust the pattern rather than any one result.

## Test 1: The Water Test

Break off a piece about the size of your thumbnail. Drop it into a glass of warm water and stir gently. Wait two or three minutes and look at the bottom of the glass.

![Water test showing pure jaggery dissolving clear and adulterated jaggery leaving sediment at the bottom of the glass](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-water-test-pure-vs-adulterated.jpg "Left: our sakhar after three minutes. Right: a market sample bought the same week.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | The water turns brown and cloudy, then clears as the piece dissolves. Nothing is left sitting at the bottom.
Adulterated | A white, grey or gritty layer settles at the bottom, or a film floats on top.
:::

**Why it works.** Cane sugar dissolves in water; chalk, sand and stone powder do not. They are heavier than water and simply fall. It is the same principle behind the household adulteration tests in the [FSSAI DART booklet](https://fssai.gov.in/book-details.php?bkid=201).

## Test 2: The Colour Test

This is the myth worth breaking first. Bright golden-yellow jaggery is not the good stuff. In most cases that shade has been helped along with a clarifier or a dye.

Natural sakhar runs from deep brown to almost black-brown. It also changes from batch to batch. The same field, boiled two weeks apart, gives two different browns.

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Dark brown, matte, slightly uneven in colour across the block.
Adulterated | Uniform bright yellow or orange, often with a glossy surface.
:::

![Comparison of natural dark brown jaggery and bright yellow chemically treated jaggery side by side](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/dark-jaggery-vs-yellow-jaggery.jpg "Same weight, same price, very different processing.")

### Is dark jaggery better than yellow, and what does jaggery colour actually mean?

Yes, in general, but not because dark is magic. Colour is a record of how the juice was treated. Long, slow boiling over wood darkens the sugars naturally, so a dark block usually means nothing was added to stop that happening.

A pale block means the darkening was prevented. Sometimes that is careful skimming by hand. More often it is a clarifier.

**Why it works.** You are not judging the colour itself. You are judging what the colour tells you about the boiling.

## Test 3: The Taste Test

Break a small piece and let it melt on your tongue instead of chewing it. Pure sakhar is clean and sweet, with a mild caramel or smoky note at the end.

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Sweet, round, a faint caramel finish. Nothing lingers.
Adulterated | A salty edge, a bitter finish, or a flat chemical taste that stays in your mouth.
:::

**Why it works.** Excess salt is a sign the juice was over-treated during boiling, and bitterness usually comes from a clarifier that did not wash out. Your tongue notices both long before any instrument would.

## Test 4: The Iodine Test for Starch

This is the only test that needs something from the pharmacy. It is also the most conclusive. Dissolve a piece of sakhar in a little warm water, let it cool, then add two drops of tincture of iodine.

![Iodine test on jaggery solution to detect added starch](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-iodine-starch-test.jpg "Two drops of tincture of iodine is all it takes.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | The solution stays brown. The iodine colour fades into it and nothing else happens.
Adulterated | The solution turns blue, blue-black or dark purple within seconds.
:::

**Why it works.** Iodine reacts with starch and turns dark blue. There is no starch in sugarcane juice, so any blue means something starchy was added for weight: flour, rice powder or arrowroot.

It is a standard household check, and the method is set out in the [FSSAI manual of quick adulteration tests](https://fssai.gov.in/).

## Test 5: The Hardness Test

Press a corner of the block with your thumb, then try to break a piece off with your fingers. You are testing how it gives way, not how strong you are.

![Testing jaggery hardness by crumbling a piece by hand](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-hardness-texture-test.jpg "Pure sakhar crumbles along a grain rather than snapping clean.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Firm, but it yields under your thumb and crumbles with a slightly grainy edge.
Adulterated | Glassy and crystal-hard. It shatters into sharp pieces instead of crumbling.
:::

**Why it works.** Added sugar syrup crystallises as the block cools, and crystals shatter. Natural sakhar keeps a little moisture and molasses in it, so it stays firm rather than brittle.

## Test 6: The Rub Test

Wet your fingertips, take a small piece and rub it between them until it starts to melt. Then look at your fingers.

![Rub test checking jaggery for chalk powder residue on wet fingers](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/jaggery-rub-test-chalk-residue.jpg "Sticky is normal. Powdery white is not.")

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Clean, sticky and syrupy. Your fingers go brown and rinse clean.
Adulterated | A dry white or grey powder stays behind after the sticky part has melted away.
:::

**Why it works.** Sugar melts with warmth and moisture. Chalk and washing soda do not. They stay on your skin as a powder once everything around them has dissolved.

## Test 7: The Smell Test

Warm a piece in your hand for a few seconds, then hold it close to your nose. Do this before the taste test, while your senses are still fresh.

:::compare
Pure sakhar | Boiled sugarcane, a little woodsmoke from the fire, a hint of molasses.
Adulterated | Sharp, sour or faintly chemical. Sometimes there is no smell at all.
:::

**Why it works.** Smell is the first thing that goes when juice is over-processed. A block that smells of nothing has usually been stripped of the compounds that make sakhar smell like sakhar.

If you would rather run these with something keeping track, we have put the seven tests into a [sakhar purity test you can work through](/tools/sakhar-purity-test). It records what your block did and reads the results together at the end.

## How to Identify Pure Jaggery in Two Minutes

If someone in your house asks for the *sakhar chinne tarika*, the short way to know, it is this:

- Glass of warm water: does it leave sediment?
- Colour: bright yellow, or honest dark brown?
- Taste: clean and sweet, or salty and bitter?
- Iodine: does it go blue?
- Thumb: does it crumble, or shatter like glass?
- Wet fingers: sticky, or powdery white?
- Nose: sugarcane and smoke, or nothing?

![Checklist infographic of the 7 home tests to identify pure jaggery](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/7-tests-pure-jaggery-checklist.jpg "Save this to your phone before your next shop.")

## Real vs Fake Jaggery: What Our Hill Sakhar Looks Like

We make [our chemical-free hill sakhar](/products/organic-jaggery-block) in Sankhuwasabha. The cane grows on hill terraces without chemical fertiliser or pesticide. What that hill method changes about the block in your hand, and how it differs from Terai gur, is set out in [what makes Himalayan jaggery different](/blog/himalayan-jaggery-sankhuwasabha). The juice is pressed in a kolhu, boiled in an iron kadhai over a wood fire, and poured into wooden moulds, with no sulphur, no clarifier, no colour and no added sugar.

![Traditional kolhu and iron kadhai making chemical-free sakhar in the Nepali hills](/blog/how-to-identify-pure-jaggery-sakhar/traditional-jaggery-making-kolhu-nepal.jpg "The kadhai our sakhar is boiled in. Nothing goes into the juice but time and fire.")

Here is how it does against the same seven tests, honestly.

It dissolves clean, with no sediment. It stays brown under iodine. It tastes of caramel and a little smoke, it crumbles under a thumb, and it leaves your fingers sticky rather than chalky.

Now the parts we would rather not advertise. **The colour changes every batch.** Some blocks are the colour of dark chocolate, others closer to red-brown. That is the cane and the fire, not a mistake.

**It is not glossy.** A pure block looks rough and dull next to a polished market one. On the shelf, it honestly looks like the cheaper product.

**It softens in the monsoon.** In humid months it can go sticky at the edges or sweat slightly in the packet. That is moisture, and it is what unrefined sakhar does when nothing has been added to stop it.

The first time we ran the water test side by side with a market sample, our glass went brown and cleared, and theirs left a grey ring at the bottom that would not stir away. That is the day this article started.

We hold no organic certificate yet, and we would rather say that plainly than imply one. What we can tell you is how it is made and how it behaves in your glass. If you are looking for chemical-free jaggery in Nepal, you now have seven ways to check any of it, including ours.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How can I tell if jaggery is pure?

Dissolve a piece in warm water and look for sediment, then check the colour, the taste and the smell. Pure sakhar dissolves fully, is dark brown rather than bright yellow, tastes clean and sweet, and smells of boiled cane and woodsmoke. Run three tests, not one.

### Why is some jaggery dark brown and some light yellow?

Colour comes from how long the juice was boiled and whether anything was added to keep it pale. Slow wood-fired boiling darkens sugar naturally, giving deep brown. Bright, even yellow usually means a clarifier or a dye was used, or that the batch was blended with refined sugar.

### Does pure jaggery dissolve completely in water?

Yes. Cane sugar is fully water-soluble, so a piece of pure sakhar disappears into warm water leaving only brown colour behind. A gritty or chalky layer at the bottom of the glass means an insoluble filler such as chalk, sand or stone powder is present.

### Is hard jaggery better than soft jaggery?

No, hardness tells you about moisture and sugar, not quality. Glassy, crystal-hard jaggery that shatters often contains added sugar syrup. Pure sakhar is firm but crumbly and softens in humid weather, so soft is normal in monsoon and glass-hard rarely is.

### What chemicals are added to jaggery?

The common ones are clarifiers such as sulphur and washing soda, artificial colours such as metanil yellow, chalk powder as a bulking agent, and refined sugar syrup for weight and hardness. Not all are food grade. None of them are added for your benefit.

### Is shiny, bright jaggery bad?

It is a warning sign, not proof. A glossy, evenly bright block has usually been treated to look that way, because shoppers reward golden jaggery. Test it before you trust it: the water test and the iodine test will tell you far more than the shine will.

## Before You Buy Your Next Block

Pure sakhar is darker, plainer and less perfect-looking than the version most shops sell. It varies between batches, it does not shine, and it softens when the air is wet. Once you know that, the polished golden block stops looking like the better buy.

You do not need to take anyone's word for it, including ours. Water, colour, taste, iodine, thumb, fingers, nose: seven tests, ten minutes, one glass. That is how to identify pure jaggery, and it works on whatever brand is in front of you.

Once you trust the block, the next two questions are usually what it is worth and what to do with it. We have answered both: [how sakhar compares with white sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar) on calories, minerals and blood sugar, and [how to make jaggery tea without curdling the milk](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling), which is where most people abandon the swap. If somebody in the house has diabetes, start instead with [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics).

If you would like to run the seven tests on ours, [see the organic jaggery we make in Nepal](/shop), or [message us](/contact) and we will send a small piece to test against whatever is in your cupboard.
