**यी सङ्ख्या कहाँबाट आए।** यी हामीले आफ्नै पोकामा छाप्ने र उत्पादनको पृष्ठमा राख्ने सङ्ख्या हुन्, प्रयोगशालाको परीक्षणमा होइन, हाम्रा ढिक्का भण्डारणमा कस्ता रहन्छन् भन्ने अनुभवमा आधारित। प्रयोगशालामा हामीले जाँच गराएका छैनौं। ढिक्काअनुसार बनोट र चिस्यान फरक पर्छ भन्ने कुरा [Sugar Tech को समीक्षा](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) र [नन-सेन्ट्रिफ्युगल उखुको चिनी](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar) को विवरणमा छ। कहिल्यै कुनै ब्याच प्रयोगशालामा पठायौं भने, मन नपरेका भागसहित, नतिजा यहीँ राख्नेछौं।

दुवै सङ्ख्या माथिको भण्डारण मानेर लेखिएका हुन्। साउनभरि टेबलमा खुला छोडेको ढिक्का केही हप्तामै टाँसिन सक्छ, र अँध्यारो दराजको बन्द भाँडोमा राखेको ढिक्का मितिभन्दा धेरै टिक्छ।

## ढुसी, सेतो धुलो कि दाना: सख्खरमा के उम्रियो?

भण्डारण गरेको ढिक्कामा चार कुरा देखिन्छन्, र तीमध्ये दुईको मात्र अर्थ सकियो भन्ने हो।

:::compare
मसिनो सेतो धुलोजस्तो तह | चिस्यान चल्दा सतहमा चिनी दाना बनेर निस्केको। हानिरहित। झारिदिनुहोस् वा वास्ता नगर्नुहोस्, र बिर्को जाँच्नुहोस्।
तल जम्मा भएको टाँसिने चासनी | माथि भनेजस्तै तानिएको चिस्यान। ढिक्का पहिलेभन्दा भिजेको छ। सख्खरकै गन्ध आउँछ भने प्रयोग गर्नुहोस्।
खरानी, हरियो, निलो वा कालो भुवा | ढुसी। तपाईंले पस्न दिएको चिस्यान चाहिएको थियो। खुर्केर बाँकी नराख्नुहोस्, र बहस नगर्नुहोस्। ढिक्का सकियो।
अमिलो, खमिरजस्तो वा रक्सीजस्तो गन्ध | किण्वन, अर्थात् खमिरले काम गर्न पुग्ने जति पानी थियो। यो पनि सकियो, र स्वादमा पनि थाहा हुन्छ।
:::

हामी सख्खर बनाउने हौं, खाद्य सुरक्षा निकाय होइनौं। इमानदार नियम त्यही पुरानो हो जुन हरेक भान्सालाई थाहा छ: ठीक छ कि छैन भनेर उभिएर सोच्दै हुनुहुन्छ भने, जोखिम लिनु लायक छैन। फाल्नुहोस्।

## सख्खरको धुलो राख्ने काम फरक हो

धुलो उही सख्खर हो, तर सतह धेरै गुणा बढी, त्यसैले माथिका सबै कुरा यसमा छिटो हुन्छन्। यो टाँसिने डल्लोभन्दा पनि पोकाको कुनामा एउटै इँटाजस्तो जम्छ।

आएको पोका बन्द हुँदा ठीक हुन्छ, खोलेपछि कमजोर। सानो हावा नछिर्ने भाँडामा सार्नुहोस्, अँध्यारो ठाउँमा राख्नुहोस्, र हरेकपटक सुक्खा चम्चा प्रयोग गर्नुहोस्। भिजेको चम्चा धुलोमा फर्कनु नै धेरैजसो भाँडो जम्ने कारण हो।

जमिसकेको छ भने बिग्रिएको होइन। चम्चाको पिठ्युँले फुटाउनुहोस्, र पहिलेजस्तै घुल्छ। [चियाका लागि धुलो सजिलो](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling) हुनुको एउटा कारण यही हो।

## नरम भएको ढिक्का बचाउन सकिन्छ?

प्रायः सकिन्छ, गन्ध ठीक छ र केही उम्रिएको छैन भने।

साँचो हावा नछिर्ने भाँडामा सारेर केही दिन अँध्यारो, सुक्खा ठाउँमा राख्नुहोस्। सतहको चिस्यान मिल्दै जाँदा कडा हुन्छ। मङ्सिरमा जस्तो कडा सुक्खा ढिक्का फेरि हुँदैन, र हुनु पनि पर्दैन।

नभए बनावटको मतलब नहुने ठाउँमा प्रयोग गर्नुहोस्, जुन धेरैजसो ठाउँ हो। नरम सख्खर सजिलै कोरिन्छ, कडा ढिक्काभन्दा चियामा छिटो घुल्छ, र [माघे सङ्क्रान्तिको चाकु](/ne/blog/chaku-kasari-banaune) का लागि राम्रैसँग पग्लन्छ। टड्कारो आवाज हराएको ढिक्काले भाँडामा चाहिने केही हराएको छैन।

## बारम्बार सोधिने प्रश्नहरू

### सख्खर लामो समय कसरी राख्ने?

हावा नछिर्ने, अँध्यारो, चिसो र सुक्खा। कसिलो बिर्को भएको सिसा वा स्टिलको भाँडो, दराजको पछाडि, चुलो र झ्यालबाट टाढा। ठूलो ढिक्कालाई पहिले नै टुक्रा पार्नुहोस्, ताकि दिनहुँ भाँडो खोल्नु नपरोस्।

### सख्खर फ्रिजमा राख्नुपर्छ?

पर्दैन, र वर्षको धेरैजसो समय फ्रिजबाहिरै राम्रो। हावा नछिर्ने भाँडोमा चिसो, अँध्यारो दराज पुग्छ। बर्खाको सबैभन्दा ओसिलो बेलामा फ्रिज ठीकै हो, तर कोठाको तापक्रममा नआउञ्जेल भाँडो बन्दै राख्नुहोस्।

### मेरो सख्खर किन टाँसियो?

हावाबाट चिस्यान तान्यो। सेतो चिनीबाट हटाइने मोलासेस सख्खरमा बाँकी रहन्छ, र त्यसले पानी तान्छ। यो बिग्रनु होइन, भण्डारणको समस्या हो, र सुक्खा दराजको बन्द भाँडोले प्रायः ठीक पार्छ।

### सेतो ढुसी लागेको सख्खर खान मिल्छ?

मिल्दैन। सेतो भुवा ढुसी हो र ढिक्का फाल्नुपर्छ। मसिनो सुक्खा धुलोजस्तो तह भने फरक हो, त्यो सतहमा चिनी दाना बनेको हो र हानिरहित छ। भुवा भुवा नै हो। शङ्का लाग्यो भने फाल्नुहोस्।

### खोलेपछि सख्खर कति टिक्छ?

हाम्रो ढिक्का ६ देखि १२ महिना र धुलो ६ महिना भनेर बेचिन्छ, माथि भनेजस्तै राख्दा। राम्ररी राखे त्यति टिक्छ। बर्खाभरि पोकामै खुला छोडे केही हप्तामै टाँसिन सक्छ, तर टाँसिनु र खान नमिल्नु एउटै होइन।

### सख्खरको म्याद सकिन्छ?

ताजा खानाजस्तो सकिँदैन, किनभने यति गाढा चिनीमा थोरै मात्र कुरा उम्रन्छन्। ढिक्कालाई सक्ने चिस्यान हो: धेरै भयो भने ढुसी वा किण्वन हुन्छ, र त्यसपछि सकियो। सुक्खा राखे सख्खर भान्साको सबैभन्दा क्षमाशील चिजमध्ये एक हो।

### सख्खर र धुलो एउटै भाँडामा राख्ने?

नराख्नु राम्रो। दुवैले फरक गतिमा चिस्यान लिन्छन्, र ढिक्का नरम हुनुभन्दा धेरै अघि धुलो डल्लो पर्छ। दुई साना भाँडाले दुवैलाई राम्रो राख्छन्।

## त्यसो भए सख्खर कसरी राख्ने?

सिसामा, अँध्यारोमा, बन्द गरेर, टुक्रा पारेर, चुलोभन्दा टाढा। पूरा जवाफ यति हो, र यसको मूल्य एउटा भाँडो हो।

बाँकी अपेक्षाको कुरा हो। सख्खर रिफाइन्ड हुँदैन, किन्नुको कारण पनि यही हो र यसरी व्यवहार गर्नुको कारण पनि यही। बर्खामा नरम हुन्छ, सुक्खा महिनामा कडा हुन्छ, र नेपाली बर्खाभरि पटक्कै नफेरिने ढिक्काले आफ्नैबारे केही भनिरहेको हुन्छ।

नयाँ किलो सुरु गर्दै हुनुहुन्छ भने आएकै दिन भाँडोमा टुक्रा पारेर राख्न लायक [१ किलोको ढिक्का](/ne/products/organic-jaggery-block) हो। [२५० ग्रामको धुलो](/ne/products/jaggery-powder) झन् सजिलो, पोकाबाट निकालेपछि।

अनि हामी सबै कुराको अन्तमा भन्ने कुरा: जुनसुकै भाँडामा होस्, चाहेभन्दा कम खानुहोस्। [WHO ले थपिएको चिनी दैनिक करिब २५ ग्रामभन्दा कम](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children) राख्न सुझाव दिन्छ, र सख्खर चिनीजस्तै त्यसभित्र गनिन्छ। राम्ररी राखेको किलो धेरै दिन टिक्नुपर्छ। टिकेन भने त्यो पनि ध्यान दिन लायक कुरा हो।

अङ्ग्रेजीमा यही लेख [यहाँ](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar) छ।

title: Is Jaggery Safe in Pregnancy? An Honest Answer, Sutkeri Included
seoTitle: Is Jaggery Safe in Pregnancy? An Honest Answer
description: Is jaggery safe in pregnancy? An honest answer from a sakhar maker on iron, gestational diabetes, the hot food belief and jaggery in sutkeri after birth.
author: Rashmita Bhandari
authorBio: Rashmita founded SakharSansar in 2024 and runs it end to end — she tends the wood fire, pours the moulds and packs every block by hand. The cane comes off the terraces her family and forty-one neighbouring households farm in Sankhuwasabha, the way they have made sakhar for seven generations.
imageAlt: A block of Nepali hill sakhar, in an article on whether jaggery is safe in pregnancy
content:
The advice arrives before the scan does. A mother-in-law with a steel box of sakhar. An aunt on the phone saying jaggery builds blood. A neighbour who says it is too hot for a pregnant woman and should be stopped at once. Three people who love you, three different rules, and all of them about the same brown block.

We make sakhar (सख्खर), or jaggery, in the hills of Sankhuwasabha, and "is jaggery safe in pregnancy?" reaches us more often than almost any other question. We are producers, not doctors or midwives. So this page will tell you what sakhar actually is, which of the family rules hold up, and which questions belong with the person looking after your pregnancy.

> Jaggery in pregnancy is ordinary food. In normal amounts it is no more dangerous than any other sugar, and no more beneficial either. It is not a source of iron worth counting, it does not treat anaemia, and it raises blood sugar like sugar does. If you have gestational diabetes or are being treated for anaemia, follow your clinician, not a jar.

## Is Jaggery Safe During Pregnancy?

For most people, in ordinary amounts, yes, in the same way that sugar in your chiya is safe. There is nothing in sakhar that makes it harmful to a pregnancy, and nothing that makes it protective.

Sakhar is sugar cane juice with the water boiled out. What is left is mostly sucrose, with some glucose and fructose, a little moisture and a small mineral fraction. The [Sugar Tech review of non-centrifugal sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) sets out how that composition varies between batches. None of it behaves differently because you are pregnant.

What changes in pregnancy is not the jaggery. It is how closely your blood sugar, your weight and your iron are being watched, and those are the three places where the family advice tends to go wrong.

## Does Jaggery Increase Iron or Haemoglobin?

This is the claim we hear most, and it is the one we would most like to put down gently.

Sakhar does keep a trace of the iron that refining strips from white sugar. A trace is the right word. To get a meaningful amount of iron from jaggery you would have to eat a quantity of sugar that would be bad for anyone, pregnant or not. We have gone through the arithmetic in [the benefits people claim for sakhar](/blog/jaggery-health-claims-truth).

Anaemia in pregnancy is common, and it is taken seriously for good reason. It is found with a blood test and treated with what your antenatal clinic gives you, usually iron tablets, sometimes more. If you have been given iron, sakhar is not a replacement for it and not a reason to take less of it.

We know that sounds like a jaggery maker talking people out of jaggery. It is. On this one question, believing the label can cost someone their health, and we would rather lose the sale.

## Can Jaggery Cause Gestational Diabetes?

Sakhar does not cause gestational diabetes on its own, any more than one sweet does. But it is sugar, it raises blood glucose the same way white sugar does, and if you have been diagnosed with gestational diabetes it has to be counted exactly as sugar is.

There is no such thing as a jaggery that is safe for diabetes, in pregnancy or out of it. The full, honest answer is in [whether sakhar is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics). If you have been told your sugar is high, your clinician is the place to start, and that article is the second.

## Is Jaggery "Hot" for a Pregnant Woman?

Many Nepali families divide food into hot and cold, and sakhar goes firmly in the hot column. That is why one relative will tell you to eat it for strength and another will tell you to stop.

This is a traditional belief, and we would label it as one. There is no good evidence that jaggery raises body heat in a way that affects a pregnancy, or that it causes miscarriage or early labour in ordinary amounts. If a particular food is worrying you or someone in the family, ask at your next check-up. A two-minute answer from a midwife settles more arguments in a household than any article.

## How Much Jaggery Is Reasonable in Pregnancy?

The same limit that applies to everyone. The World Health Organization's [guideline on sugars intake](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028) recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of daily energy, and suggests a further benefit [below about 25 grams, or six teaspoons, a day](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children).

Sakhar is a free sugar and counts inside that total, alongside the sugar in chiya, sweets and biscuits. A teaspoon of [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) in a cup of tea fits comfortably. A tray of chaku every afternoon does not, whatever it is made of.

If your clinician has given you a different target, theirs wins.

## What About Sakhar After the Birth?

In many Nepali homes, a new mother in her sutkeri weeks is fed rich, warm food: ghee, jwano, meat broth, and sweets made with sakhar. The tradition is old and it comes from care. For a woman who has just given birth, a household that cooks for her is worth more than any single ingredient on the plate.

What the tradition often says about sakhar, that it cleans the womb, builds blood or brings in milk, is traditional belief rather than established fact. We would not repeat those claims on a label, and we would not ask a new mother to rely on them. The same honest rule applies: sakhar is food, it counts as sugar, and anything medical, including bleeding, anaemia or blood sugar, goes to the person looking after her.

If you are cooking for someone in sutkeri and she likes the taste, a [sakhar block](/products/organic-jaggery-block) grated into her food is a kind thing to do. Just do it because she likes it.

## What If You Crave Jaggery?

Cravings in pregnancy are common and not a sign that your body needs sugar in particular. If you want something sweet, a small piece of sakhar is as reasonable a choice as any other sweet, and more satisfying than most because the taste is strong.

If you find yourself wanting a great deal of it, or wanting non-food things like soil or ice, mention it at your next appointment. Unusual cravings are sometimes linked to low iron, which is one more reason to get the iron checked properly rather than treat it with jaggery.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is jaggery safe during pregnancy?

In ordinary amounts, yes. It is food, and it counts as sugar. Nothing in sakhar harms a pregnancy in normal quantities, and nothing in it protects one either. Gestational diabetes and anaemia are the two situations where you should follow your clinician's advice on sugar.

### Does jaggery increase haemoglobin in pregnancy?

Not in any meaningful way. Jaggery keeps only a trace of iron, and you would need a harmful amount of sugar to get a useful dose. Anaemia in pregnancy is treated with iron from your antenatal clinic, and jaggery is not a replacement.

### Can I eat jaggery if I have gestational diabetes?

Only as counted sugar within the plan your doctor or dietitian has given you. Jaggery raises blood glucose like white sugar does. There is no jaggery that is safe for diabetes.

### Is jaggery hot for pregnancy?

The idea that jaggery is a "hot" food is a traditional belief. There is no good evidence that ordinary amounts affect a pregnancy through body heat. If it worries you, ask your midwife or doctor.

### How much jaggery can a pregnant woman eat in a day?

It counts towards the same free sugar limit as everyone else, which the WHO suggests keeping below about 25 grams a day. A teaspoon in chiya fits. If your clinician has set a different limit, follow theirs.

### Is jaggery good after delivery?

It is a traditional part of sutkeri food in many Nepali homes, and it is fine as food. Claims that it cleans the womb, builds blood or increases breast milk are traditional beliefs, not established facts.

### Is jaggery better than sugar in pregnancy?

Not for your health in any way that matters. Jaggery is unrefined and has a stronger taste, so you may use less of it. It is still sugar, and the full comparison is in [sakhar vs sugar](/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar).

## The Short Answer

Eat sakhar in pregnancy if you enjoy it, in the amounts you would eat any sugar. Do not eat it for iron, for blood, or because someone said it is medicine. Take the real questions, sugar and iron especially, to the people looking after you.

If you want to know who makes ours and how, [this is the story](/our-story).

This article is general information about food, not medical advice. Your midwife or doctor knows your pregnancy. We only know the jaggery.

title: Gud vs Misri: What Is the Difference, and Which Is Better?
seoTitle: Gud vs Misri: The Difference, and Which Is Better
description: Gud vs misri: how jaggery and rock sugar are made, how they differ in taste, colour and minerals, and when misri is honestly the better choice.
author: Rashmita Bhandari
authorBio: Rashmita founded SakharSansar in 2024 and runs it end to end — she tends the wood fire, pours the moulds and packs every block by hand. The cane comes off the terraces her family and forty-one neighbouring households farm in Sankhuwasabha, the way they have made sakhar for seven generations.
imageAlt: A block of dark sakhar, the gud of the Nepali hills, compared with misri
content:
At a temple in the Valley the prasad comes as small white crystals of misri, clear as glass. At home, the same grandmother who offered it breaks off a piece of dark sakhar after dal bhat. Two sweets, both from cane, both called healthy by somebody, and one question we are asked about them over and over: which is better, gud or misri?

We make sakhar (सख्खर), which is the gud (गुड) of the hills, in Sankhuwasabha. We do not make misri. That puts us on one side of this comparison, so we will say plainly where misri is the better choice.

> Gud (jaggery, sakhar) is cane juice boiled down and set with its molasses kept in. Misri (मिश्री) is sugar syrup crystallised slowly into clear lumps, which makes it close to pure sucrose. Gud tastes of caramel and keeps a trace of minerals. Misri is cleaner and milder. Both are sugar and both raise blood sugar the same way.

## What Is Misri?

Misri is crystallised sugar. A concentrated sugar syrup is left to cool slowly, often on threads or in shallow trays, and large clear crystals grow out of it. It is sold as irregular lumps or as crystals still strung on the thread they grew on.

Because it is grown from syrup rather than set from whole juice, misri is almost entirely sucrose. That is what makes it clear. Some misri is made from refined white sugar, and some from less refined syrup, which gives it a faint yellow tint.

In Nepal and across South Asia it turns up as temple prasad, as a mouth freshener with saunf after a meal, and in home remedies for a sore throat.

## What Is Gud?

Gud, gur, sakhar: one product, different words depending on where you stand. In the Terai and across the border it is gud or gur. In the hills it is sakhar. In English it is jaggery. We have set out every name in [what sakhar is called in English and Hindi](/blog/sakhar-in-english).

It is sugar cane juice, pressed and boiled in an open pan until most of the water has gone, then poured to set. Nothing is spun out. The molasses, the glucose and fructose and the small mineral fraction all stay in the block. That is why it is brown, why it tastes of caramel and woodsmoke, and why it goes sticky in the monsoon.

## Gud vs Misri: The Comparison

:::table Gud (jaggery) and misri side by side
Question | Gud / sakhar | Misri
How it is made | Whole cane juice boiled down and set | Sugar syrup crystallised slowly
Mostly made of | Sucrose, plus glucose, fructose, molasses | Almost pure sucrose
Colour | Golden to dark brown, varies by batch | Clear to pale yellow
Taste | Caramel, deep, sometimes smoky | Clean, mild sweetness
Minerals | A trace | Close to none
Raises blood sugar | Yes | Yes
Keeps in the monsoon | Softens and goes tacky | Stays hard and dry
Best used for | Chiya, chaku, kheer, sel roti, winter sweets | Prasad, saunf, clear syrups, anything that must stay pale
:::

**Where these facts come from.** The composition of jaggery follows the [Sugar Tech review of non-centrifugal sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) and the general description of [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar). Misri, being crystallised sucrose, sits close to the USDA entry for [granulated sugar](https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/portal-data/external/169655). We have not had either product laboratory tested ourselves, so we give no figures of our own.

## Is Gud or Misri Healthier?

Neither, in any way your body will notice.

Gud keeps a trace of iron, potassium and magnesium that misri does not. That trace is real and it is small. You would need to eat a harmful amount of sugar to get a useful amount of any mineral out of it, which is the point we make in [the benefits people claim for sakhar](/blog/jaggery-health-claims-truth).

Misri is often described as "cooling" and gud as "heating". That is a traditional way of sorting food, not something that shows up in how either sugar is digested. Label it as tradition and enjoy it as tradition.

Both are free sugars under the [WHO guideline on sugars intake](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028), and both count in full. If diabetes is in the picture, neither is a safe swap for the other, and [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics) explains why.

## Is Misri Good for a Cough?

Misri with black pepper, or with saunf, is a common home remedy for a sore throat. Sucking on something sweet does soothe a scratchy throat for a while, and that comfort is real.

It is not a treatment. A cough that lasts, a fever, or trouble breathing needs a doctor, and no sugar, clear or brown, changes that. The same applies to sakhar in hot water with ginger, which is the version many hill households make instead.

## When Should You Use Misri Instead of Gud?

This is the part that costs us the sale, and it is worth saying.

- **When the colour matters.** A pale kheer, a clear syrup, a white sweet. Gud will turn all of them brown.
- **When the taste should stay quiet.** Misri sweetens without adding flavour. Gud always adds its own.
- **For prasad and saunf.** Tradition asks for misri, and there is no reason to change it.
- **In a humid store.** Misri keeps hard through a Nepali monsoon. Gud needs an airtight jar, as we explain in [how to store sakhar](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar).

## When Is Gud the Better Choice?

- **In chiya**, where its stronger taste means a smaller spoon does the same work.
- **In chaku, sel roti, kheer and winter sweets**, which were built around its flavour in the first place.
- **When you want an unrefined sweetener** with no bleaching and nothing added, made in [small batches over a wood fire](/our-story).

For those, a [sakhar block](/products/organic-jaggery-block) for cooking and [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) for the cup cover almost everything.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the difference between gud and misri?

Gud is cane juice boiled down and set with its molasses kept in, so it is brown and tastes of caramel. Misri is sugar syrup crystallised slowly into clear lumps, so it is almost pure sucrose and tastes mildly sweet.

### Which is better, gud or misri?

For health, neither in any meaningful way, since both are sugar. For cooking, gud suits chiya, chaku and winter sweets, and misri suits prasad, saunf and anything that must stay pale.

### Is misri the same as sugar?

Very nearly. Misri is crystallised sucrose, the same sugar as white sugar, grown into larger crystals. Some misri is made from less refined syrup and has a slight yellow tint.

### Is misri cooling and gud heating?

That is a traditional way of classifying food. There is no good evidence that either changes body heat. Both are sugar and both are digested the same way.

### Is misri good for diabetes?

No. Misri is almost pure sucrose and raises blood glucose like white sugar. Neither misri nor gud is a safe sugar substitute for someone with diabetes.

### Is misri or gud better for a cough?

Both are traditional comforts for a sore throat, and a sweet in the mouth does soothe it for a while. Neither treats a cough. A lasting cough or fever needs a doctor.

### What is misri called in English?

Rock sugar or crystal sugar. In Nepali and Hindi it is मिश्री, misri or mishri.

## The Verdict

Gud and misri are two shapes of the same thing: cane sugar. One kept everything the cane gave it, and one was grown into clear crystals from almost nothing but sucrose. Choose by taste and by what you are cooking. Do not choose by health, because neither one earns it.

Whichever you pick, use a little less than the recipe says.

title: Til Ko Laddu: Sesame Laddu With Sakhar for Maghe Sankranti
seoTitle: Til Ko Laddu Recipe With Jaggery for Maghe Sankranti
description: How to make til ko laddu with sakhar for Maghe Sankranti: roasting the til, the soft ball test, shaping by hand, and why laddu fall apart or set hard.
author: Rashmita Bhandari
authorBio: Rashmita founded SakharSansar in 2024 and runs it end to end — she tends the wood fire, pours the moulds and packs every block by hand. The cane comes off the terraces her family and forty-one neighbouring households farm in Sankhuwasabha, the way they have made sakhar for seven generations.
imageAlt: A block of sakhar broken for til ko laddu, sesame and jaggery sweets for Maghe Sankranti
content:
On the morning of Maghe Sankranti the plate comes round with chaku, ghee, tarul, and a small heap of til ko laddu (तिलको लड्डु), round and knobbly and still smelling of the pan. Somebody made them the night before with hands greased in ghee, rolling each one fast before the syrup set, and swearing gently at the hot ones.

Til ko laddu is the easiest Sankranti sweet to make at home, and the one most people get slightly wrong. We make the sakhar (सख्खर), or jaggery, that binds them, in the hills of Sankhuwasabha, and this is how we would explain it across a kitchen counter.

> Til ko laddu is roasted sesame bound with melted sakhar (jaggery) and rolled into balls, made for Maghe Sankranti. Roast the til, melt the sakhar with a little ghee and water until a drop in cold water forms a soft ball, stir in the til, and shape the laddu with greased hands while the mixture is still warm.

## Ingredients

- 200 g white sesame seeds (til)
- 200 g sakhar block, broken into small pieces
- 1 tablespoon ghee, plus more for your hands
- 2 tablespoons water
- 50 g roasted peanuts, roughly crushed (optional)
- 2 green cardamom, seeds crushed (optional)

This makes about 15 to 18 laddu the size of a walnut.

## Which Jaggery Works for Til Ko Laddu?

A firm, dry [sakhar block](/products/organic-jaggery-block) is the right choice. It melts cleanly and sets the laddu firm without going sticky in a warm room. A very soft, wet block carries extra water into the pan, so the syrup takes longer to reach the right stage and the laddu stay tacky.

[Sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) works and melts faster. It also catches faster, so keep the heat lower if you use it. We have not tested the two side by side under controlled conditions, so take that as a cook's view.

## Method

### Step 1: Roast the til

Dry roast the sesame in a heavy pan over a low flame, stirring all the time, until the seeds turn a shade darker, start to pop and smell nutty. This takes about five minutes.

Tip them onto a plate straight away. Sesame keeps cooking in a hot pan and turns bitter within a minute of being done.

### Step 2: Melt the sakhar

In the same pan, put the broken sakhar, the ghee and the water over a low to medium flame. Stir until the sakhar has melted completely and there are no lumps left.

Do not raise the heat to hurry it. Jaggery scorches at the bottom of the pan long before the top has melted.

### Step 3: Cook to the soft ball stage

Let the syrup bubble gently, stirring, for a few minutes. It will foam, settle and thicken.

Drop a little into a bowl of cold water. When it gathers into a soft ball you can press between your fingers, it is ready. If it dissolves and clouds the water, keep going. If it snaps like glass, it has gone too far, and the laddu will be very hard. This is a softer stage than chaku, which needs a longer cook.

### Step 4: Stir in the til

Take the pan off the heat. Tip in the roasted sesame, the peanuts and cardamom if you are using them, and stir quickly until every seed is coated.

### Step 5: Shape the laddu

Grease your palms with ghee. While the mixture is still warm, take a spoonful and press and roll it firmly into a ball. Work fast, and re-grease your hands every few laddu.

If the mixture sets before you finish, put the pan back on the lowest flame for a few seconds to soften it. If it is too hot to handle, wet your palms with cold water instead of ghee for a moment, then carry on.

### Step 6: Let them set

Lay the laddu on a greased plate and leave them for about half an hour, until they are firm all the way through.

## Why Til Ko Laddu for Maghe Sankranti?

Maghe Sankranti falls in mid-January and marks the turn of the winter. The food eaten that day is chosen for the cold: chaku, til, ghee, tarul, sweet potato. Til and sakhar together are the heart of it, and laddu are the simplest way to put the two in one mouthful.

Til ko laddu and chaku sit on the same plate but they are built the other way round. In a laddu, the sesame is the body and the jaggery is only the glue. In chaku, the jaggery is the body, worked until it pales, with sesame folded through. If you want the harder of the two, our [chaku recipe](/blog/chaku-recipe-maghe-sankranti) walks through it.

## Why Til Laddu Go Wrong

**They will not hold together.** The syrup came off before the soft ball stage. Put the mixture back on a low flame, cook a little longer and test again.

**They are rock hard.** The syrup went past soft ball towards hard crack. Still edible, just hard on the teeth. Take it off sooner next time.

**They taste bitter.** Either the sesame over-roasted or the sakhar scorched. Neither can be fixed. Roast til on the lowest flame and melt sakhar slowly.

**They go sticky after a day.** Humidity, or a soft, wet block of jaggery. Store them airtight, and use a firmer block next time.

## How Much Sakhar Do You Need?

The recipe uses equal weights of til and sakhar. Scale from there.

:::table How much sakhar to buy for til ko laddu
Til | Sakhar | Roughly how many laddu
200 g | 200 g | 15 to 18
500 g | 500 g | 40 to 45
1 kg | 1 kg | 80 to 90
:::

One 1kg block makes a large batch of laddu, or a batch of laddu and a batch of chaku together, which is what many households make for Sankranti.

## How to Store Til Ko Laddu

In an airtight box at room temperature, away from steam. They keep well for a couple of weeks. What ends them is moisture, which makes the jaggery go tacky. Our [guide to storing sakhar](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar) explains why jaggery behaves that way.

Do not refrigerate them. Condensation forms on the surface every time the box comes out.

## The Honest Note About Eating It

Til ko laddu is sesame and sugar. The sesame is a real food, with fat, protein and fibre. The sakhar is a sweetener, and being unrefined [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar) does not change that. The [WHO advice on free sugars](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children) counts it the same as white sugar, and the [full guideline](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028) explains why.

Two laddu on Sankranti morning is a festival. A box a day through Magh is a sugar habit. If diabetes is in the family, read [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics) before the plate goes round.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do you make til ko laddu with jaggery?

Roast sesame until it pops, melt jaggery with a little ghee and water until a drop in cold water forms a soft ball, stir in the sesame, and roll the mixture into balls with greased hands while it is still warm.

### What is the ratio of til to jaggery for laddu?

Equal weights is the usual starting point, for example 200 g of sesame to 200 g of sakhar. Use a little less jaggery for a drier, nuttier laddu.

### Why are my til laddu not binding?

The jaggery syrup was not cooked long enough. It needs to reach the soft ball stage. Warm the mixture again on a low flame, cook it a little further and test a drop in cold water.

### Why are my til laddu too hard?

The syrup was cooked past the soft ball stage. Take it off the heat as soon as a drop in water forms a ball you can squash.

### What is the difference between til ko laddu and chaku?

In til ko laddu the sesame is the main ingredient and jaggery only binds it. Chaku is mostly jaggery, cooked to the thread stage and worked with ghee, with sesame folded in.

### How long do til laddu last?

About two weeks in an airtight box at room temperature, away from moisture. Do not keep them in the fridge.

### Can I use jaggery powder for til laddu?

Yes. It melts faster, which helps, but it scorches faster too, so keep the flame low and stir from the start.

## One Last Thing

Make them the evening before Sankranti, while somebody else is making the chaku, and let the youngest person in the house shape a few. They will be lopsided. They always are, and they are always eaten first.

If you want to know where the sakhar in them comes from, [this is our story](/our-story).

title: Peanut Chikki With Sakhar: Jaggery Brittle That Actually Snaps
seoTitle: Peanut Chikki Recipe With Jaggery (Sakhar)
description: How to make peanut chikki with sakhar: roasting the peanuts, cooking jaggery to the hard crack stage, rolling it thin, and why homemade chikki turns chewy.
author: Rashmita Bhandari
authorBio: Rashmita founded SakharSansar in 2024 and runs it end to end — she tends the wood fire, pours the moulds and packs every block by hand. The cane comes off the terraces her family and forty-one neighbouring households farm in Sankhuwasabha, the way they have made sakhar for seven generations.
imageAlt: A block of hill sakhar ready to melt for peanut chikki
content:
The best test of peanut chikki is the sound. Snap a piece and it should crack cleanly, like thin ice, not bend and not stick to your teeth. Most homemade chikki fails that test the first time, and almost always for the same reason: the jaggery came off the fire a minute too early.

Chikki is a hard brittle of roasted peanuts set in jaggery, sold in wrappers at every bus park and tea shop from the Terai to the hills. It is also one of the easiest things to make with a block of sakhar (सख्खर). We make that sakhar, or jaggery, in the hills of Sankhuwasabha. Here is how to get the snap right.

> Peanut chikki is roasted peanuts bound in jaggery cooked to the hard crack stage, rolled thin and cut into squares. Roast and skin the peanuts, melt sakhar with a spoon of ghee, cook it until a drop in cold water snaps, stir in the peanuts, then roll the mixture thin on a greased surface and cut it while warm.

## Ingredients

- 200 g raw peanuts (badam)
- 200 g sakhar block, broken into small pieces
- 1 tablespoon ghee, plus more for greasing
- 1 tablespoon water
- A small pinch of baking soda (optional)

This makes one tray, about 20 pieces.

## Which Jaggery Works for Chikki?

A hard, dry [sakhar block](/products/organic-jaggery-block). Chikki needs the jaggery taken further than any other sweet on this site, to the hard crack stage, and a dry block gets there faster and more reliably. A soft, wet block has to boil off its extra water first, and it is more likely to scorch while it does.

[Sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) will work, with a lower flame, because it catches quickly. For chikki we would reach for the block.

Darker, wood-fired sakhar makes a darker chikki with a deeper, slightly smoky taste. That is the flavour of the jaggery, not a sign you burned it. Burnt chikki tastes bitter, which is different.

## Method

### Step 1: Roast and skin the peanuts

Dry roast the peanuts in a heavy pan over a medium-low flame, stirring, until the skins crack and the nuts smell roasted, about eight to ten minutes. Tip them onto a cloth, let them cool a little, then rub them in the cloth to loosen the skins.

Blow or sift away the skins. Split the peanuts in half with a rolling pin if you like a flatter chikki.

### Step 2: Prepare the surface

Grease a steel tray, the back of a thali, or a clean kitchen counter with ghee. Grease a rolling pin too. You will not have time to do this once the jaggery is ready.

### Step 3: Melt the sakhar

Put the sakhar, the ghee and the water in a heavy pan over a low flame and stir until it has melted into a smooth, glossy syrup with no lumps.

### Step 4: Cook to the hard crack stage

Let it bubble, stirring, as it foams, darkens and thickens. This takes several minutes, longer than for chaku or laddu.

Test it often. Drop a little into cold water and take it out. At the hard crack stage it sets instantly and snaps cleanly between your fingers. If it bends or feels chewy, it is not ready. This is the whole recipe, so be patient here.

If you are using baking soda, stir it in now. The syrup will foam up and lighten, which makes the chikki a little more crisp and a little less hard on the teeth.

### Step 5: Add the peanuts

Take the pan off the heat and tip in the peanuts. Stir fast until every nut is coated. The mixture will start to stiffen almost at once.

### Step 6: Roll and cut

Turn it out onto the greased surface. Flatten it with the greased rolling pin to about half a centimetre thick, working quickly.

Cut it into squares with a greased knife while it is still warm. Once it cools, it will shatter rather than cut. Leave the pieces to cool completely, about fifteen minutes, then break them apart.

## Why Chikki Goes Wrong

**It is chewy and sticks to the teeth.** The syrup never reached hard crack. There is no fixing a set tray, but next time cook longer and trust the cold water test over the clock.

**It tastes bitter.** The jaggery scorched. The heat was too high or the pan too thin. Start again with a heavier pan and a lower flame.

**It is too thick to bite.** It was not rolled while hot enough. Have the surface and rolling pin ready before the syrup is.

**It went soft after a few days.** Moisture got in. Chikki pulls water out of the air the way jaggery does, which is why it comes in sealed wrappers. Our guide to [storing sakhar](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar) explains the chemistry.

## Chikki, Badam Chaku and Til Laddu: What Is the Difference?

All three are nuts or seeds held in jaggery, and they are cooked to different points.

- **Til ko laddu** is sesame bound by jaggery at the soft ball stage, rolled by hand. The softest of the three. Our [til ko laddu recipe](/blog/til-ko-laddu-sakhar) has the method.
- **Badam chaku** is chaku, jaggery cooked to the thread stage and worked with ghee until it pales, with peanuts folded in. Chewy and dense. The method is in our [chaku recipe](/blog/chaku-recipe-maghe-sankranti).
- **Chikki** is jaggery taken all the way to hard crack, so it sets glassy and snaps. The hardest of the three.

The ingredients are almost the same. The temperature is what changes everything.

## How Much Sakhar Do You Need?

The recipe uses equal weights of peanuts and sakhar.

:::table How much sakhar to buy for peanut chikki
Peanuts | Sakhar | Roughly how many pieces
200 g | 200 g | About 20
500 g | 500 g | About 50
1 kg | 1 kg | About 100
:::

## How to Store Chikki

In an airtight tin, at room temperature, with paper between the layers. Kept dry, it stays crisp for a couple of weeks. In the monsoon, keep the tin tightly shut and away from the stove.

## The Honest Note About Eating It

Peanuts are a real food. The jaggery around them is sugar, unrefined [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar) that keeps a little more of the cane than white sugar does, and nothing more than that. Chikki is often sold as a healthy snack because of the peanuts and the word jaggery. It is a sweet, and the [WHO guideline on sugars](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028) counts the jaggery in it exactly as it counts white sugar, with a suggested limit of [about 25 grams of free sugar a day](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children).

A piece with chiya is a pleasure. If diabetes is part of the picture, read [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics) first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do you make peanut chikki with jaggery?

Roast and skin peanuts, melt jaggery with a little ghee, cook it to the hard crack stage so a drop in cold water snaps, stir in the peanuts, roll the mixture thin on a greased surface and cut it while warm.

### Why is my chikki chewy and not crisp?

The jaggery did not reach the hard crack stage. Keep cooking until a drop in cold water sets instantly and snaps between your fingers.

### What is the ratio of peanuts to jaggery in chikki?

Equal weights is the usual ratio, for example 200 g of peanuts to 200 g of sakhar. Use a little less jaggery for a nuttier chikki.

### Why add baking soda to chikki?

A small pinch makes the syrup foam and trap air, so the chikki is a little lighter and easier to bite. It is optional.

### How long does chikki last?

About two weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature. Humidity softens it, so keep it sealed.

### Is chikki healthy?

It is a sweet. The peanuts bring fat, protein and fibre, but the jaggery is sugar and counts as sugar. Enjoy it in small pieces.

### Can I make chikki with jaggery powder?

Yes, but it scorches faster than a block, so use a low flame and stir constantly. A hard, dry block is easier for chikki.

## One Last Thing

Your first tray will probably be a little chewy. The second one will snap. Keep a glass of cold water by the stove and trust it more than the clock.

If you want to know who makes the sakhar and how, [this is our story](/our-story).

title: Jaggery in Winter: Why Nepal Eats Sakhar in Poush and Magh
seoTitle: Jaggery in Winter: Is Sakhar Really Hot for the Body?
description: Why Nepal eats jaggery in winter, whether sakhar is really a hot food, what it does for a winter cold, and the Poush and Magh dishes built around it.
author: Rashmita Bhandari
authorBio: Rashmita founded SakharSansar in 2024 and runs it end to end — she tends the wood fire, pours the moulds and packs every block by hand. The cane comes off the terraces her family and forty-one neighbouring households farm in Sankhuwasabha, the way they have made sakhar for seven generations.
imageAlt: A block of fresh winter sakhar from Sankhuwasabha, made when the cane is cut in Mangsir
content:
In Sankhuwasabha the cane comes in with the cold. It is cut in Mangsir, the fire under the kadhai goes on before first light, and the steam off the boiling juice is the warmest thing on the terrace until the sun clears the ridge. Sakhar (सख्खर), or jaggery, is a winter food in Nepal twice over: it is made in winter, and it is eaten in winter.

Ask anyone why and you will hear the same answer: sakhar is garam, hot, and it keeps the body warm through Poush and Magh. We make it for a living, and we have heard that line our whole lives. This article is about what is true in it, what is tradition, and how Nepali kitchens actually use jaggery in the cold months.

> Jaggery is eaten in winter in Nepal because it is made then, because the festivals of the season are built around it, and because tradition calls it a "hot" food. That last idea is a belief, not a measured effect. Sakhar gives energy like any sugar, and it tastes good in a cold kitchen. It does not warm the body in a way sugar does not.

## Why Is Jaggery Eaten in Winter?

Three reasons, and only one of them is about the body.

**It is the season.** Sugar cane is harvested in late autumn and early winter, and the crushing and boiling happen then. For most of Nepal's history, fresh sakhar was a winter thing because that is when there was any. Our own batches come off the fire from Mangsir onwards.

**The festivals are in winter.** Yomari Punhi in December, Maghe Sankranti in January. The foods of both are built on jaggery: chaku, til, yomari filled with it. A season's calendar has a way of becoming its diet.

**It is dense energy for cold days.** Sugar is quick energy, and on a cold morning a warm, sweet drink feels right. That is real, and it is true of any sugar, not especially of jaggery.

## Is Jaggery Hot for the Body?

In the traditional way of sorting food into hot and cold, yes. Sakhar, ghee, til and meat are hot. Curd, cucumber and misri are cold. The system is old and it shapes what Nepali families cook in every season.

It is worth being clear about what that means. Jaggery is [non-centrifugal cane sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-centrifugal_cane_sugar), mostly sucrose with some glucose, fructose and a trace of minerals, as the [Sugar Tech review of non-centrifugal sugar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314846/) sets out. There is no good evidence that jaggery raises body temperature, improves circulation, or protects against colds in a way that white sugar does not. When you eat any food, your body produces a little heat digesting it, and a warm drink warms you while you drink it. That is the honest size of the effect.

We would label "sakhar keeps you warm" as tradition, the same way we label the other claims in [the benefits people claim for sakhar](/blog/jaggery-health-claims-truth). Tradition is worth keeping. It is not the same as a measured result.

## Does Jaggery Help With Winter Colds?

Sakhar in hot water with ginger, or with tulsi and black pepper, is what many Nepali households make when someone has a cold. The warm drink soothes a sore throat and keeps fluids up, and that comfort is real.

It does not treat the infection, and it does not stop you catching one. A fever that will not go down, a cough that lasts for weeks, or any trouble breathing needs a doctor, especially for a child or an older person. For children, there is more detail in [whether jaggery is good for children](/blog/jaggery-for-children).

## How Do Nepalis Use Jaggery in Winter?

Mostly the way they always have.

- **Chiya with sakhar.** The cold-morning cup. Dissolve the sakhar before the milk goes in or it will curdle, which is explained in [how to make jaggery tea without curdling](/blog/jaggery-tea-without-curdling).
- **Hot water with sakhar and ginger.** The winter drink for when you feel unwell or simply cold.
- **Chaku for Maghe Sankranti.** Jaggery, ghee and sesame, worked until it pales. Our [chaku recipe](/blog/chaku-recipe-maghe-sankranti) walks through it.
- **Til ko laddu.** Sesame bound with jaggery, the easiest Sankranti sweet. The method is in our [til ko laddu recipe](/blog/til-ko-laddu-sakhar).
- **Yomari.** Rice-flour dumplings with a chaku filling for Yomari Punhi, in our [yomari recipe](/blog/yomari-chaku-recipe).
- **Sakhar with ghee and roti.** A plain winter breakfast in many hill homes.
- **Tarul and sweet potato.** Boiled and eaten at Sankranti, sometimes with a little sakhar or ghee.

## Is It Better to Eat Jaggery in Winter Than in Summer?

For your health, it makes no difference. Sugar is sugar in any month.

For the jaggery itself, winter is kinder. A block that stays hard and dry from Mangsir to Chaitra will start to soften and go tacky once the monsoon arrives, because it pulls water out of the air. That is why [how to store sakhar](/blog/how-to-store-jaggery-sakhar) matters more in Asar than in Magh.

If you buy a year's worth in winter, break it down into airtight jars before the rains.

## How Much Jaggery Is Reasonable in Winter?

The same as the rest of the year. The World Health Organization's [guideline on sugars intake](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028) suggests keeping free sugars low, with a further benefit [below about 25 grams a day](https://www.who.int/news/item/04-03-2015-who-calls-on-countries-to-reduce-sugars-intake-among-adults-and-children). Jaggery counts inside that total exactly as chini does.

Winter is the season when that limit is easiest to forget. Chaku on the counter, laddu in the tin, sweet chiya three times a day. None of it is harmful on a festival morning. All of it adds up across Magh. If diabetes is in the family, read [whether jaggery is safe for diabetics](/blog/is-jaggery-safe-for-diabetics) before the season starts.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why do we eat jaggery in winter?

In Nepal, because it is made in winter when the cane is harvested, because the winter festivals of Yomari Punhi and Maghe Sankranti are built around it, and because tradition considers it a warming food.

### Is jaggery hot or cold for the body?

In the traditional hot and cold classification of food, jaggery is hot. That is a belief rather than a measured effect. There is no good evidence that jaggery warms the body more than any other sugar.

### Does jaggery keep you warm in winter?

Not in any special way. Any food gives a little heat as it is digested, and a warm drink warms you while you drink it. Jaggery does not do more than that.

### Is jaggery good for a cold in winter?

Hot water with sakhar and ginger soothes a sore throat, and that comfort is real. It does not treat the cold. See a doctor for a high fever, a lasting cough or trouble breathing.

### What is the best way to eat jaggery in winter?

In chiya, in hot water with ginger, with ghee and roti, and in the Sankranti sweets: chaku and til ko laddu. Keep the amounts small, because sweet things pile up quickly in the festival season.

### Can I eat jaggery every day in winter?

A small amount, yes, counted inside the same sugar limit as the rest of the year. The WHO suggests keeping free sugars below about 25 grams a day.

### When is jaggery made in Nepal?

Mostly in late autumn and winter, when the sugar cane is harvested. Our cane is cut from Mangsir, and the batches are boiled over a wood fire from then on.

## The Short Version

Eat sakhar in winter because it is the season, because the festivals ask for it, and because it tastes right in a cold kitchen. Do not eat more of it because someone said it will keep you warm. A shawl does that better.

If you want this winter's batch, the [1kg sakhar block](/products/organic-jaggery-block) is for chaku and cooking, and [sakhar powder](/products/jaggery-powder) is for the cup. You can read about [the terraces and the fire it comes from](/our-story).

The fire under our kadhai is lit before light for most of the winter. On the coldest mornings, it is the best place on the hill to stand.
